guide.title: Pacing, quotas and why we queue
guide.subtitle: Sending slower on purpose, to send more overall
guide.excerpt: Every connection carries a send rate. The platform queues to that rate instead of firing as fast as a provider will accept, because the fastest way to get throttled is to send at the speed that causes it.

p: A connection has a send rate, expressed as messages per second. When a batch is running, the platform releases messages to the provider at that rate rather than submitting everything at once.

The default per provider is deliberately conservative. It is a starting point, not a statement about your account — your real ceiling is set by your provider, based on your account level, the number type and the destination country.

This is the part worth getting right: providers generally rate-limit per sending number, not per account or per connection. If a connection has several sender numbers bound to it, the effective capacity is roughly the per-number rate multiplied by the number of numbers.
So the value on a connection has to be set with the number count in mind. Leaving it at the default when you have bound five numbers is not cautious, it is slow for no reason.

When a provider pushes back because a request arrived too fast, that is a pacing signal, not a broken send. The platform backs off and retries the message rather than marking it failed and moving on. Marking a throttled message as failed would produce a retry storm against an already-congested provider, which is exactly the situation that escalated the throttling in the first place.

sections.h: Two rates, and the lower one wins
p: There are two separate rates in play. The subscription tier sets a submit rate — how fast you may hand messages to the platform. The connection sets a send rate — how fast the platform calls your provider.
Whichever is lower governs. Raising the plan submit rate does not raise your provider quota, and raising the connection rate does not bypass the plan.

list: Knowing your actual provider quota, including whether it is per number or per account.
Any destination-specific registration your provider requires before it will carry traffic to that country.
Choosing how many sender numbers to bind to a connection, which is what actually sets the ceiling.
